https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/a.text: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home World News Warsaw, Kyiv exhume Volyn massacre victims at center of diplomatic quarrel AFP, OSTRIVKY, Ukraine Add TT as Preferred Source Beneath two now-deserted villages in western Ukraine — the site of World War II-era massacres — archeologists are uncovering the bones at the heart of a dispute that has strained relations between Warsaw and Kyiv for years. Disagreements over what happened and who is responsible for the Volyn massacres have long cast a shadow over ties between the otherwise now close neighbors. Between 1943 and 1945, about 70,000 to 100,000 civilians were killed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) in territory occupied by Nazi Germany, according to Polish estimates of the toll. Archeologists work with human remains at the exhumation site of the World War II Volyn massacre near the destroyed village of Ostrivky, Ukraine, on Tuesday. Photo: AFP Warsaw calls it a “genocide” against the Polish minority, while Ukraine hails the UPA as freedom fighters, sees the events as a wartime “tragedy” and says that Ukrainians were killed in retaliation. Amid sunflower fields and forests, joint Polish-Ukrainian teams of archeologists have been carefully excavating the remains of victims. “We want to restore their first and last names ... to fulfill the duty that rests on us as heirs of those who were murdered here,” Polish Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) deputy president Karol Polejowski said. The remains of more than 50 people have been recovered in a series of exhumations in the area, but they have yet to be identified. A handmade wooden cross, planted near the graves, is one of the few signs that the villages ever existed. Political leaders in both countries believe the exhumations could be a first step in repairing relations, which have been strained this year by a row triggered when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy named a military unit after the UPA. In a white tent about 10km from the Polish border, experts meticulously lay out the skeletons of recovered victims, measuring bones and carefully trying to match broken skull fragments. A small number of other artifacts — rosaries, religious medallions and shoes — have also been unearthed under the field of yellow-and-black sunflowers, one of the national symbols of Ukraine. “The remains were arranged in a highly disordered manner. Most of the bodies had been brought to the burial pit and simply dumped into it,” Ukrainian Memorial and Search Center anthropologist Olga Mineiko said. Polejowski said the victims were likely “driven to the field of death barefoot and without personal belongings.” The genetic material is collected, with the IPN appealing to Poles who believe they might have lost relatives in the massacre to provide their own to help find matches. Forensic specialists and anthropologists would also examine the bones to determine the approximate age, sex and cause of death of each of them. It is believed that between 30 to 40 percent of the 50 remains discovered so far were children, Polejowski said. The massacres have been a recurring point of contention between Warsaw and Kyiv. The UPA was a paramilitary organization tied to the Ukrainian independence movement that fought the Soviet Union’s Red Army. However, it collaborated with the Nazis when they first invaded the Soviet Union, clashed with the Polish resistance, and killed Poles, Jews and other civilians. Since Russia invaded in 2022, the UPA has been honored in Ukraine as a force that fought for independence from Moscow under the Soviet Union. Kyiv insisted Zelenskiy’s choice of name for the military unit was not directed against Warsaw, but Polish President Karol Nawrocki withdrew Poland’s highest national honor from him in response. In Poland, the issue has become even more politicized as nationalist parties seek to embolden their base ahead of parliamentary elections next year — part of a broader campaign to whip up anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Poland is home to hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian refugees — with a backlash against their presence having surged during a divisive presidential election campaign last year, won by the right-wing Nawrocki. The country is still the main hub for military and humanitarian aid deliveries to Ukraine, and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s pro-European government has repeatedly called for a de-escalation. Warsaw has welcomed efforts by Zelenskiy to cool the tension, including the promise of opening of classified intelligence documents. As Tusk and Zelenskiy try to bury the hatchet, in the Ukrainian fields near the Polish border, plans are underway for a proper farewell to those uncovered. “We want them to be buried here, where they lived, where each of them had their dreams and plans, and wanted their life to unfold,” Polejowski said. “In this soil they should rest.” Most Popular 1 First tax refunds to be deposited on Friday 2 Taiwan suspends visa processing for Moroccans 3 Notes from Central Taiwan: Institutionalizing Taiwan’s tourism failure 4 AIT hails joint coast guard operations 5 PLA building more Taiwan mock-ups You might also like Major brands sell China tomatoes as Aussie-grown: ABC 2026-07-28 Several major food brands in Australia are selling tomato products grown in China as domestically produced, with forensic testing showing some are sourced from the Xinjiang region, an investigation by the Australian Broadcasting Corp (ABC) said. https://aldergrovestar.com/2026/09/25/po.text: News Regional News Election Video Wildfires News Tips Business Community Life Travel West Coast Traveller Today’s Home Entertainment Contests Readers’ Choice Puzzles Events Sports Opinion Letters Submit Letter to the Editor Obituaries In Memory Place An Obituary Public Notices Classifieds All Classifieds Place a classified ad eEdition Special Sections Home Services About Us Contact Us Submission Forms Newsletter Sign-Up Join Our Team eEdition Special Sections News Regional News Election Video Wildfires News Tips Business Community Life Travel West Coast Traveller Today’s Home Entertainment Contests Readers’ Choice Puzzles Events Sports Opinion Letters Submit Letter to the Editor Obituaries In Memory Place An Obituary Public Notices Classifieds All Classifieds Place a classified ad Polish ukulele teacher becomes eager student at Langley festival Published 5:45 pm Friday, September 25, 2026 By Heather Colpitts Poland’s Bart Orlowski met Langley-born ukulele player James Hill when Hill was in Poland and it changed the direction of Orlowki’s life. “I started doing my own ukulele school in my city, Szczecin,” he said. “Now there’s a huge community. After six years of activity, it’s amazing what happens now, and it’s still happening, and I have so many plans for the future.” Orlowski, who has never been to Hawaii, was here for the second Fort Langley International Ukulele Festival from Sept. 22 to 26, taking in as much as he could from some of the world’s most renowned players. He was thrilled to be able to meet the man who got Hill into the unique instrument – Peter Luongo, who started the Langley Ukulele Ensemble four decades ago. Soon after starting the ensemble, the Langley players went to Hawaii, where they were so well received, they had standing invitations for many years. “My first trip there with kids was back in 1985,” Luongo said. The Langley Ukulele Ensemble carries on under the direction of his son, Paul. It has groups based on age and skill level that perform around this community but also around B.C. and farther afield, including summer 2026 shows in England. Orlowski has been bands over the years and was working as a sound engineer before quitting to start his own school. His students eagerly awaited his return to learn from the talent that came to Langley because of the international reputation of the Langley Ukulele Ensemble. “Ukulele is the most social instrument I’ve ever seen, and it brings people together,” Orlowski said. “The guitar says ‘ Watch me and listen to me. The ukulele says ‘ Come and play along with me.’ It’s so beautiful.” The festival featured free performances, concerts, and sold-out workshops on everything from songwriting and chord progressions to instrument makers and how to play jazz on a ukulele. The public can head to the salishan Place by the River amphitheatre in Fort Langley for a day of ukulele with performances, jam sessions, vendors, Polynesian history, and more. There’s the Premiere Concert at the Chief Sepass Theatre with international talent, and a jam session at the Fort Langley Community Hall from 9:30 to 11 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 26. The festival also brought together uke players with B.C.’s Polynesian community. The Hudson’s Bay Co. had many Hawaiians working for them in centuries past with their ancestors still sharing their traditions with fans. Taking part in the festival were dancers with the Hālau Hula KaʻUhane O Ka Pakipika (Spirit of the Pacific) school, which also teams up with the Fort Langley National Historic Site for an annual summertime celebration of local Polynesian history. • READ MORE: Langley Ukulele Ensemble at the 30-year mark • READ MORE: Music from the soul fuels London trip You Might Like Elderly Langley pilot surprised with special flight Langley trustee candidate advocated homeschooling PLAYER’S DIARY: Hungry heading towards playoffs Former Langley Mountie given no jail time in assault case News Business Community Life Entertainment Sports Opinion Obituaries Public Notices Video Press releases Classifieds Submission Forms eEdition Newsletter Sign-Up Events Contact Us About Us Advertising Join Our Team
